# Retrieval: Search Before Generation {#sec-retrieval}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The measurements extend @sec-turkish-nlp's
retrieval experiment — the same 7,165 Turkish documents, the same query
construction, the same seed — so the sparse numbers here and there are
directly comparable. Two query conditions and two dense models are used
deliberately; @sec-retrieval-conditions says why running only one of each
would have measured the wrong thing. Software: `sentence-transformers` 6.0.0,
`snowballstemmer` 3.1.1, NumPy 2.5.2 on Python 3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- build a BM25 baseline and say precisely which queries it wins;
- explain what a dense retriever adds, and construct a query type where it
  beats lexical search by seventy points and one where it loses by sixty;
- decide whether to fuse two retrievers, using a rule rather than a habit;
- tune the recall/latency dial on an approximate index deliberately;
- report retrieval quality with recall@k and nDCG, and know which of them
  bounds what your downstream system can possibly do.

## Two families, and the question that decides between them {#sec-retrieval-families}

Retrieval has two families and they fail in opposite directions.

**Lexical retrieval** matches words. BM25 — the standard scoring function
[@robertson2009probabilistic] — is @sec-text-as-data's TF-IDF with two
corrections that matter: term frequency **saturates**, so the tenth occurrence
of a word adds far less than the second, and document length is normalised, so
a long document does not win by containing more of everything. (The formula,
and what its two knobs $k_1$ and $b$ do, is written out in
@sec-retrieval-interview.)

It is fast, exact, interpretable, needs no training, and it cannot match a word
it has never seen.

**Dense retrieval** matches meaning. A
[bi-encoder](#gloss-bi-encoder){#term-bi-encoder .term-ref}
[@karpukhin2020dense] embeds queries and documents separately into the same
space, so documents can be encoded once and searched by vector similarity
(usually the cosine similarity of @sec-embeddings). It handles paraphrase, synonymy and — as this chapter will show — different
languages.

It needs a trained model, it cannot guarantee an exact match on a part number,
and its failures are hard to explain.

::: {#gloss-bi-encoder .column-margin .term-gloss}
**bi-encoder** — query and document encoded independently, so every document
can be embedded ahead of time and search is a vector lookup. The independence
is what makes it scale, and what limits its accuracy relative to a
cross-encoder. [↩](#term-bi-encoder){.term-back}
:::

The received framing is that dense is the modern one and lexical is the
baseline you report out of politeness. The measurements below say something
less convenient.

**What we will look at.** First the experiment, which needs two query
conditions rather than one, because a single condition would have measured the
query format and blamed the model. Then the results, where the same two
systems swap places by sixty points and hybrid fusion — the thing everyone
recommends — costs more than either parent alone. Then how a dense retriever
is trained, where the hard negatives are the whole game. Then reranking, the
approximate index, and the four metrics, one of which is a ceiling on
everything downstream. And finally where to put the vectors, which is a
smaller question than it is usually made to be.

## The experiment, and why it has two conditions {#sec-retrieval-conditions}

@sec-turkish-nlp measured the sparse side on 7,165 Turkish documents: with
queries whose terms are inflected differently from the document — the case
where a user types the dictionary form — surface-form BM25 reaches 28.0%
recall@1 and stemming takes it to 95.3%.

The obvious next step is to add a dense retriever to that setup and see. **The
obvious next step is also a trap**, and it is worth spending a paragraph on
because the same trap is available in any retrieval evaluation you build.

Those queries are *three disconnected content words*. That is the natural
input for a lexical matcher and it is out of distribution for a bi-encoder
trained to embed sentences. Running only that condition and reporting "dense
retrieval is weak in Turkish" would have been measuring the query format and
blaming the model.

So the experiment runs **two query conditions** against the same documents:

| condition | the query is | who this favours |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **A. keyword, inflected** | three content words, in a different inflection than the document uses | lexical matching, if it can handle morphology |
| **B. cross-lingual** | the document's professional English translation | dense only — there is no shared vocabulary at all |

: Two conditions, chosen so neither family gets a home advantage
{tbl-colwidths="[24,44,32]"}

And **two dense models**, for the same reason:
`paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM` is a *similarity* model, trained to score how
alike two sentences are, and `multilingual-e5-base` [@wang2024e5] is a
*retrieval* model, trained on query-document pairs with hard negatives.
Reaching for the first because it is the famous one is a common mistake, and
running only it would have understated dense retrieval.

**One instruction from E5's model card that this chapter should have recorded
and did not.** `multilingual-e5-base` is an *asymmetric* retrieval model: it is
trained with a `query: ` prefix on queries and a `passage: ` prefix on
documents, and the card is explicit that it behaves measurably worse without
them. This is exactly the setting where the prefixes matter most — an
asymmetric query-document task is what they exist for — and it is the most
common silent error in an embedding pipeline; @sec-clustering makes the same
point for the symmetric case, where the card prescribes `query: ` on both sides.
Our runs do not state which convention they used. If the prefixes were omitted,
E5's numbers below are measured under a setting its own card advises against —
which is a reason to re-run rather than a guarantee that the scores would rise
or that both of this chapter's headline margins would shrink. Treat the E5 rows
as pending that check, and record the prefixes beside the model name when you
run this.

Two upstream decisions this experiment sidesteps, so that you do not miss
them in your own system. First, what counts as a "document": here every
document is a single sentence, but real documents are longer and have to be
cut into chunks before they are embedded, and the best chunk size depends on
the kind of question (@sec-rag-chunking measures it). Second, for Turkish
BM25, lowercase with Turkish rules: Python's default `lower()` turns `I` into
`i` instead of `ı` and `İ` into `i` plus a combining dot, which mangles words
before stemming ever runs (@sec-turkish-nlp-normalization).

## What the measurements say {#sec-retrieval-results}

Both conditions run against the same corpus, so the two tables below are
directly comparable — and the point is how little they have in common. 800
queries per condition, 7,165 documents, and **one relevant document per query
by construction** — each query is built from one target document and that
document is treated as the only correct answer.

That last assumption is not verified, and it is not symmetric. On 7,165
sentences of news text, three content words will often describe more than one
sentence, and the system that surfaces a near-paraphrase is precisely the dense
one — so unlabelled relevant documents push dense recall@1 down more than
BM25's. The fix is the one this chapter's own interview section prescribes: pool
the top-10 of every system on a subsample and label the union by hand. We did
not do it. Until someone does, read condition A's dense numbers as a floor
rather than an estimate.

Two things to know before reading the tables. First, the columns. **R@1** and
**R@10** are recall@1 and recall@10; with one relevant document per query they
simply ask "is the right document first?" and "is it anywhere in the top
ten?". MRR@10 and nDCG@10 also reward a high position, and all four are defined
properly in @sec-retrieval-metrics. Second, the *hybrid* rows. They combine a
BM25 ranking and a dense ranking with
[reciprocal rank fusion](#gloss-rrf){#term-rrf .term-ref} (RRF)
[@cormack2009reciprocal]. Every document gets the score
$\sum_s 1/(k + \text{rank}_s(d))$, summed over the systems $s$ that returned
it, and the fused list is sorted by that score. A document a system did not
return adds nothing from that system. $k$ is a smoothing constant; the original
paper used $k = 60$, and it remains the common default.

::: {#gloss-rrf .column-margin .term-gloss}
**reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)** — merge several ranked lists by giving each
document $\sum 1/(k + \text{rank})$ over the lists and re-sorting. It uses
only ranks, never scores, so it needs no calibration — and it cannot tell a
strong system's first place from a weak system's.
[↩](#term-rrf){.term-back}
:::

### Condition A — keyword queries, inflected

This is the condition lexical matching should win, provided it can handle
Turkish morphology:

```text
system                                        R@1    R@10   MRR@10  nDCG@10
BM25 surface form                           27.5%   54.1%     34.9     39.4
BM25 stemmed                                96.0%   99.8%     97.7     98.2
dense: paraphrase-MiniLM (similarity model) 10.6%   28.2%     15.6     18.6
dense: multilingual-e5-base (retrieval)     35.9%   63.7%     44.5     49.1
hybrid RRF (unweighted), surface + e5       37.6%   71.6%     47.6     53.3
hybrid RRF (unweighted), stemmed + e5       63.2%   96.5%     73.7     79.2
```

[Stemmed BM25 wins by sixty points.]{.hl} A few hundred lines of hand-written
suffix-stripping rules beat a trained multilingual retriever 96.0% to 35.9% — and beat the
similarity model, the one most people reach for first, 96.0% to 10.6%.

The surface-form and stemmed rows reproduce @sec-turkish-nlp's 28.0% and 95.3%
on a slightly different query sample, which is the continuity check that lets
the rest of the table be read against it.

### Condition B — cross-lingual queries

Now the same documents, queried in English. There is no shared vocabulary for
a lexical matcher to work with:

```text
system                                        R@1    R@10   MRR@10  nDCG@10
BM25 surface form                           23.2%   43.5%     28.9     32.3
BM25 stemmed                                23.8%   41.9%     29.1     32.1
dense: paraphrase-MiniLM (similarity model) 93.8%   98.1%     95.4     96.0
dense: multilingual-e5-base (retrieval)     96.2%   99.9%     97.8     98.3
hybrid RRF (unweighted), surface + e5       49.4%   99.6%     71.6     78.7
hybrid RRF (unweighted), stemmed + e5       48.1%   99.6%     70.9     78.2
```

[Dense wins by seventy-two points.]{.hl} The English query and the Turkish
document share almost no vocabulary, so BM25 is reduced to matching proper
nouns and numbers — which is exactly why it still scores 23.8% rather than
zero, and worth noticing, because those are precisely the cases dense
retrieval is worst at.

**But say what condition B is favourable to, the way we said it for condition
A.** The query here is a *full professional translation of the document*, and
that is the most in-distribution input a multilingual bi-encoder can receive:
both of these models were trained on parallel sentence pairs, so this task is
closer to bitext mining (finding the sentence that is the translation of a
given sentence) than to search. Real cross-lingual queries are short and
question-shaped and do not cover the whole document. So read 96.2% as "dense
retrieval solves translation matching" rather than "dense retrieval solves
cross-lingual search", and read the seventy-two-point margin as an upper bound
on the dense advantage — exactly as condition A's sixty-point margin is an upper
bound on the lexical one. **Each condition hands its winner a query drawn from
the target document itself.** The missing arm is condition B′: three content
words from the *English translation*, which is condition A's cross-lingual
twin. It would put a floor under the dense margin, and it is the run we would
add first.

::: {.column-margin}
Stemming is worth **68 points** in condition A and **0.6 points** in condition
B. That is not a contradiction; it is the same fact seen twice. Stemming fixes
vocabulary mismatch *within* a language, and in condition B the mismatch is
total, so there is nothing for it to fix.
:::

### The finding that contradicts the received wisdom

Take the better of the two hybrid rows in each table (stemmed + e5 in
condition A, surface + e5 in condition B) and read it against the best single
system:

```text
condition A     stemmed BM25 alone         96.0%  R@1
                hybrid stemmed + e5        63.2%  R@1      -32.8

condition B     dense e5 alone             96.2%  R@1
                hybrid surface + e5        49.4%  R@1      -46.8
```

**Unweighted reciprocal rank fusion made things worse in both conditions**, and
badly. That is the opposite of the standard claim that hybrid retrieval beats
both parents [@cormack2009reciprocal], and the reason is visible in the
mechanism.

Be precise about what was measured, because the claim is narrower than "hybrid
retrieval is oversold". These rows are *unweighted*, *rank-based* fusion at a
constant $k$ this chapter does not report — and the widget below exists to show
you that $k$ changes the answer, which makes not reporting it a real gap.

Two standard repairs went untried. **Weighted RRF** — $\sum w_s/(k + \text{rank}_s)$
with a per-system weight fitted on held-out queries — is the obvious one, and
this chapter defers it to an exercise rather than running it. **Score-based
fusion** is the better one: @bruch2024fusion analyses exactly this question and
finds that a convex combination of normalised scores beats RRF both in and out
of domain, with a single parameter that needs very few examples to tune. So the
finding to carry is this one: *unweighted rank fusion of unequal parents is
harmful, because rank fusion throws away precisely the score-magnitude
information that would tell it which parent to trust.*

[RRF assumes the systems it is fusing are comparably good.]{.hl} It scores
each document by $\sum 1/(k + \text{rank})$ across the lists, which treats a
rank-1 hit from a useless system exactly like a rank-1 hit from an excellent
one.

When one parent is at 96% and the other at 36%, the weak parent's top-ranked
irrelevant documents arrive with full weight and displace the strong parent's
correct answer. Note that "confidence" is not the word: rank fusion never sees
a confidence score, which is exactly the information that would have told it
which parent to trust.

::: {.anlp-widget}
```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">Fuse two rankers by hand — and watch the right document lose</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rrfGoldStrong = Inputs.range([1, 10], {step: 1, value: 1,
  label: "gold document's rank in the strong system"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rrfGoldWeak = Inputs.range([1, 60], {step: 1, value: 40,
  label: "its rank in the weak system (60 = the bottom of a 60-deep list)"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof rrfK = Inputs.range([1, 60], {step: 1, value: 60, label: "RRF constant k"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// The weak system is confident about the wrong thing: it ranks a decoy first.
// The strong system has that decoy far down its own list.
rrfRows = {
  const score = (a, b) => 1 / (rrfK + a) + 1 / (rrfK + b);
  const rows = [
    {doc: "the right document", strong: rrfGoldStrong, weak: rrfGoldWeak},
    {doc: "decoy the weak system loves", strong: 20, weak: 1},
    {doc: "decoy the weak system likes", strong: 25, weak: 2},
    {doc: "decoy both systems dislike", strong: 15, weak: 15}
  ].map(r => ({...r, fused: score(r.strong, r.weak)}));
  const order = [...rows].sort((a, b) => b.fused - a.fused);
  return rows.map(r => ({...r, rank: order.indexOf(r) + 1}));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Inputs.table(rrfRows, {
  columns: ["doc", "strong", "weak", "fused", "rank"],
  header: {doc: "document", strong: "strong rank", weak: "weak rank",
           fused: "RRF score", rank: "fused rank"},
  format: {fused: v => v.toFixed(5)},
  width: {doc: 240, strong: 100, weak: 100, fused: 100, rank: 90},
  rows: 5})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
md`**${rrfRows[0].rank === 1
  ? "The right document survives at rank 1."
  : `The right document lands at rank ${rrfRows[0].rank}.`}** The strong
system ranked it ${rrfGoldStrong === 1 ? "first" : `${rrfGoldStrong}${
  rrfGoldStrong === 2 ? "nd" : rrfGoldStrong === 3 ? "rd" : "th"}`}, above
all three decoys, and it is ${rrfRows[0].rank === 1
  ? "still first among these four, even though"
  : "no longer first among these four once"} a system that is wrong gets an
equal vote.`
```
:::

Move the second slider and the mechanism becomes obvious: the weak system does
not need to be *right* to change the outcome, only to put the wrong document
at the top of its list. And notice what `k` does. A small `k` makes first
place worth far more than tenth, so each system's top hit dominates. Raising it
flattens the differences between ranks, and at the limit the fused order is
simply the order of the *summed* ranks — a document that sits in the middle of
both lists can then beat one that is first in one list and deep in the other.
Neither setting knows which system to trust.

The damage has a shape worth seeing, because it tells you when you can get
away with it:

```text
condition B     dense alone       R@1 96.2%    R@10  99.9%
                hybrid            R@1 49.4%    R@10  99.6%
```

**Recall@10 barely moved; recall@1 halved.** Fusion did not *lose* the
document — it pushed it down the list. So if your consumer reads the top ten,
the fusion cost you almost nothing; if it reads the top one, fusion cost you
half your accuracy.

All three findings fit in one picture — the swap, the fusion loss, and the
metric that hides it:

### So when should you fuse?

The rule the measurement supports, which is narrower than the folklore:

- **Fuse when the parents are comparable and fail differently.** That is the
  case @cormack2009reciprocal studied, and where fusion earns its reputation.
- **Do not fuse when one parent dominates.** Check first, on your own queries.
  It costs one evaluation run and the alternative is shipping a 47-point
  regression that every blog post told you was an improvement.
- **If your query mix contains both kinds** — and most real systems do, with
  users typing part numbers *and* asking questions — the answer is usually to
  *route* rather than to fuse: classify the query, send it to the retriever
  that handles it, and keep fusion for the genuinely ambiguous middle.

::: {.column-margin}
Weighted fusion is the obvious repair, and it is not free: the weight is a
fitted parameter, so it needs held-out queries and it will drift as your query
mix changes. Routing has the same requirement more honestly, because a router
is a model you can evaluate rather than a constant you tuned once.
:::

### And the choice of dense model matters exactly where the task is hard

One more comparison the two conditions make possible. Put the similarity model
and the retrieval model next to each other in both:

```text
                              condition A   condition B
paraphrase-MiniLM (similarity)      10.6%         93.8%
multilingual-e5-base (retrieval)    35.9%         96.2%
                                   ------        ------
                                   +25.3          +2.4
```

On the easy condition (B, for a dense model) the two are 2.4 points apart, so
a casual benchmark would conclude the model choice does not matter. On the hard
condition (A) the retrieval-trained model is **more than three times better**
(35.9% against 10.6%).

[The gap between a good and a mediocre component only appears on the inputs
that are hard for it]{.hl}, which is an argument for building the difficult
condition into your evaluation rather than reporting the average of an easy
one.

## Training a dense retriever {#sec-retrieval-training}

The models above were used off the shelf. When they are not good enough on
your domain, the training recipe is short to state and has one part that
matters far more than the rest.

A bi-encoder is trained **contrastively**: pull the embedding of a query
toward its relevant document and push it away from irrelevant ones. The loss
is usually InfoNCE over a batch. It is ordinary softmax cross-entropy in
which the "classes" are the candidate documents: score the query against the
relevant document and against several irrelevant ones, and ask the softmax to
put its probability on the relevant one. The whole difficulty is in the word
*irrelevant* — which documents you use as the wrong answers.

**In-batch negatives** are free: for a batch of query-document pairs, every
other document in the batch is a negative. They cost nothing and they are
mostly *easy* — a random document about football is not a plausible answer to
a query about invoices, so the model learns to separate topics and stops
there.

[**Hard negatives**](#gloss-hard-negative){#term-hard-negative .term-ref} are
documents that look right and are not. Mine them by retrieving with your
current model and taking the top-ranked wrong answers.

::: {#gloss-hard-negative .column-margin .term-gloss}
**hard negative** — a wrong document that looks right to the current model,
found by retrieving with it and keeping the top-ranked wrong answers. Training
against these, rather than random documents, is most of what makes a dense
retriever precise. [↩](#term-hard-negative){.term-back}
:::

[This is the whole game.]{.hl} A retriever trained only on random negatives
learns topical similarity; a retriever trained on hard negatives learns the
distinction your users actually need, which is between two documents that are
both about invoices and only one of which answers the question.

Two failure modes to plan for:

1. **False negatives.** Your "hard negative" may be an unlabelled relevant
   document, and training says it is wrong. On a corpus with sparse relevance
   labels this is common enough to hurt; the usual mitigation is to skip the
   very top of the retrieved list and mine from a little further down.
2. **Staleness.** Negatives mined with the initial model stop being hard once
   the model improves. Re-mine periodically, which is what makes this an
   iterative procedure rather than a preprocessing step.

If you have no labelled pairs at all, generate them: ask an LLM to write a
question that each document answers, and train on those. The synthetic query
is noisy on the input side and the document is genuine on the output side —
the same asymmetry that makes back-translation work in
@sec-machine-translation.

## Reranking {#sec-retrieval-reranking}

Every architecture above compares a query vector to a document vector that was
computed without ever seeing the query. There is a more accurate thing to do,
and a reason nobody does it at corpus scale.

A [cross-encoder](#gloss-cross-encoder){#term-cross-encoder .term-ref}
[@nogueira2019passage] reads the query and the document **together**, in one
forward pass with attention across both. That is strictly more informative
than comparing two independently computed vectors, and it is why a
cross-encoder is usually more accurate than a bi-encoder of similar size and
training — usually, not always: a cross-encoder trained on another domain can
still lose to a well-trained bi-encoder on yours.

::: {#gloss-cross-encoder .column-margin .term-gloss}
**cross-encoder** — query and document concatenated and read in a single
forward pass, so attention runs across both. Usually more accurate than a
bi-encoder and impossible to precompute, which is why it reranks a shortlist instead of
searching a corpus. [↩](#term-cross-encoder){.term-back}
:::

It is also unusable as a retriever. Because the score depends on the pair,
nothing can be precomputed: scoring a query against a million documents means
a million forward passes. Hence the standard two-stage pattern:

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}

On the left, the bi-encoder encodes the query and each document separately into vectors that are compared by a dot product; the document vectors are marked as computed offline, so search over a million documents costs one query encoding plus a vector operation. On the right, the cross-encoder concatenates the query and one document and reads them in a single forward pass with attention across both; nothing can be precomputed, so scoring a million documents would cost a million forward passes. Below, a pipeline shows a corpus of one million documents entering a cheap recall-oriented first stage that returns a shortlist of fifty to a hundred, then an expensive precision-oriented cross-encoder reranking that shortlist, then the top five to ten returned. ::: {.fig-cap}
The bi-encoder is fast because it never sees a pair; the cross-encoder is
accurate because it only ever sees pairs. Neither property is negotiable, so
production systems buy recall with the first and precision with the second.
:::
::::

Three consequences worth internalising:

- **The first stage sets a ceiling the second cannot raise.** A reranker can
  only reorder what it is given. If recall@50 is 80%, no reranker gets you
  past 80% — which is why @sec-retrieval-metrics argues recall@k is the metric
  to watch on stage one.
- **The cost is linear in the shortlist**, so the shortlist size is your
  quality/latency dial, and it is an easier dial than the ANN parameter: its
  cost is predictable, and the recall it hands the reranker can only grow as
  the shortlist grows. Final accuracy is another matter — it usually
  plateaus and can even dip, as step 6 of @sec-retrieval-lab explains.
- **Late interaction is the middle path.** ColBERT [@khattab2020colbert] keeps
  a vector per token and scores by summed maximum similarity (each query
  token finds its most similar document token, and those best matches are
  added up), which recovers
  much of the cross-encoder's accuracy while remaining precomputable. It costs
  an order of magnitude more storage, which is the trade.

## Approximate nearest neighbour, and the dial nobody sets on purpose {#sec-retrieval-ann}

Exhaustive search over a few thousand vectors is a matrix multiply and takes
no time at all — the dense numbers above were computed that way. At millions
of vectors it stops being free, and you move to an approximate index.

"Approximate" means the index may miss some of the true nearest neighbours in
exchange for speed. Two families dominate in practice:

**HNSW** [@malkov2018hnsw] builds a navigable graph and walks it greedily from
a coarse layer down to a fine one. Fast and accurate, memory-hungry — the
graph plus the full vectors sit in RAM.

**IVF-PQ** [@johnson2019billion] partitions the space into cells (an inverted
file, IVF: k-means clusters, each with a list of the vectors inside it),
searches only the nearest few cells, and stores *compressed* vectors via
product quantisation (PQ). PQ cuts each vector into short pieces and replaces
every piece by the index of its nearest entry in a small learned codebook. A
768-dimensional float32 vector takes 3,072 bytes; cut into 96 pieces with 256
codebook entries each, it takes 96 bytes, one per piece — 32 times smaller.
The compression is lossy in a way that costs accuracy.

Both expose a knob — `efSearch` for HNSW (how many candidates the graph walk
keeps), `nprobe` for IVF (how many cells it searches) — that trades recall
against latency. [The thing to remember is that the default is somebody
else's operating point]{.hl}, chosen for a benchmark that is not your corpus.

The discipline is the same one @sec-classification applied to a decision
threshold: sweep it, plot recall against p95 latency (the latency that 95% of
queries stay under), state your latency SLO (the service-level objective, the
latency target you have committed to), and pick the point that meets it.

And measure recall against **exhaustive search on your own data**, not against
the library's published curve — the loss depends on how your vectors are
distributed, which is a property of your corpus and your embedding model.

::: {.column-margin}
There is a trap in evaluating an ANN index against the *labels* rather than
against exhaustive search. If your recall@10 drops when you switch on the
index, you want to know whether the index lost documents or whether the
embedding was wrong to begin with. Exhaustive search is the control that
separates the two, and it is cheap to run once on a sample.
:::

## Measuring retrieval {#sec-retrieval-metrics}

Everything above was reported in four columns — recall at two depths, MRR and
nDCG — with only a one-line gloss of each. The table below adds precision@k,
which the tables did not use. These metrics answer different questions, and picking the wrong one is how a retrieval
regression stays invisible.

| metric | asks | use it when |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **[recall@k](#gloss-recall-k){#term-recall-k .term-ref}** | what share of the relevant documents is in the top *k*? With one relevant document per query — this chapter's setup — that reduces to *is it there at all*, which is also called hit rate or success@k | the consumer reads all *k* — which includes every RAG system |
| **MRR** | how high is the *first* right answer? | the user reads one result and stops |
| **nDCG@k** | are the relevant documents near the top, weighted by how relevant? | graded relevance, several relevant documents |
| **precision@k** | what share of the *k* is relevant? | the cost of a wrong result is per-result |

: Four metrics, four questions {tbl-colwidths="[16,42,42]"}

::: {#gloss-recall-k .column-margin .term-gloss}
**recall@k** — the share of a query's relevant documents that appear in the top
*k*. When there is exactly one relevant document, as here, it collapses to
*did the right document appear at all* — the quantity often called hit rate or
success@k. The number that bounds everything downstream: a generator cannot
ground an answer in a document the retriever never returned.
[↩](#term-recall-k){.term-back}
:::

The two rank-sensitive metrics are short enough to write down. For a set of
queries $Q$, let $\text{rank}_q$ be the position of the first relevant
document for query $q$:

$$
\text{MRR@}k = \frac{1}{|Q|}\sum_{q \in Q} \frac{1}{\text{rank}_q}
\quad (\text{a term counts as } 0 \text{ if } \text{rank}_q > k)
$$

$$
\text{DCG@}k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{\text{rel}_i}{\log_2(i+1)}, \qquad
\text{nDCG@}k = \frac{\text{DCG@}k}{\text{IDCG@}k}
$$

Here $\text{rel}_i$ is the relevance grade of the document at position $i$
(0 or 1 in this chapter), and IDCG@$k$ is the DCG of the best possible
ordering, so nDCG lies between 0 and 1. Some tools use the gain
$2^{\text{rel}_i}-1$ instead of $\text{rel}_i$; with 0/1 labels the two agree.

A worked example with one relevant document, as in this chapter's tables.
Suppose it comes back at rank 3. Then recall@1 = 0, recall@10 = 1, the
reciprocal rank is $1/3 \approx 0.33$, and nDCG@10 is
$1/\log_2 4 = 0.5$ (the ideal list puts it at rank 1, so IDCG = 1). Both
metrics punish rank 3, but nDCG punishes it more gently. That is why, in every
row of the tables above, nDCG@10 sits between MRR@10 and recall@10.

[If you report one number for the retrieval stage of a RAG system, report
recall@k for the *k* you actually pass to the model.]{.hl} It is a ceiling on
what *grounding* can deliver: @sec-rag's generator can only ground in what
arrives, so with one relevant document per question a retrieval recall@10 of
80% means 20% of answers cannot be grounded in retrieved evidence before
generation begins — and no amount of prompting fixes them. (Intuition check 5
below states exactly when this ceiling holds.)

The corollary is that **the two stages want different metrics**. Stage one is
judged on recall, because its job is not to miss. Stage two — a reranker, or
the generator itself — is judged on precision and ordering, because its job is
to choose. Optimising the first stage for precision@1 is a common and
expensive mistake.

Two practical notes on measurement itself:

- **You need relevance judgements, and building them is the real work.** With
  no labels, the cheapest honest start is what this chapter did: take
  documents you have, construct queries whose answer you know, and accept that
  synthetic queries are a proxy. BEIR [@thakur2021beir] is the reference
  benchmark suite if you want to compare against published numbers rather than
  measure your own corpus.
- **Report the query mix.** @sec-retrieval-results is one long argument that a
  retrieval number without its query distribution is not interpretable — the
  same two systems swap places by sixty points between two conditions on the
  same corpus.

## Vector database, or not {#sec-retrieval-storage}

The last decision is where the vectors live, and it is usually made too early
and too expensively. The honest guide is by scale:

| documents | what to use | why |
|:--|:--|:--|
| under ~100k | NumPy array plus exhaustive search | a matrix multiply; the dense numbers in this chapter were computed this way, and it is exact |
| ~100k–10M | `pgvector` in the Postgres you already run, or FAISS in-process | you get transactions, backups, joins and access control for free, and no new service to operate |
| 10M+, or multi-tenant | a dedicated vector store | when sharding, replication and filtered search stop being your problem to solve |

: Where to put the vectors {tbl-colwidths="[18,38,44]"}

[The default answer for most projects is the boring one]{.hl}: keep the
vectors next to the data they belong to.

The operational cost of a second datastore — consistency between it and your
source of truth, its own backup story, its own access-control model — is
usually larger than the query latency you were trying to save, and it arrives
on a different team's schedule.

The question that actually forces a dedicated store is rarely raw scale. It is
**filtered search at scale**: "the top 10 documents this user is allowed to
see, from the last 90 days, in Turkish." Doing that well requires the filter
and the vector search to cooperate, and that is a genuine engineering
capability rather than a matter of size.

## Intuition checks {#sec-retrieval-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. All six are questions this chapter settled
with a measurement rather than an argument.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Should you replace BM25 with a dense retriever?

Only after checking which queries you actually get. Measured on one corpus,
the same two systems swapped places by sixty points between two query
conditions: stemmed BM25 **96.0%** against dense **35.9%** on keyword queries,
and dense **96.2%** against BM25 **23.8%** cross-lingually.

Neither family dominates. Lexical wins exact-match and rare-token queries;
dense wins paraphrase, synonymy and anything crossing a language boundary.
Sample a hundred real queries and classify them before choosing.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Everyone says hybrid retrieval beats both parents. Does it?

Not when the parents are unequal. Measured here, reciprocal rank fusion **cost
32.8 points** in one condition and **46.8** in the other, against the better
parent each time.

RRF weights a rank-1 hit from a weak system exactly like a rank-1 hit from a
strong one, so the weak parent's top-ranked wrong answers displace the strong
parent's right ones. Fusion is a variance-reduction trick for *comparable*
systems. Check that yours are comparable before fusing, which costs one
evaluation run.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Your recall@10 barely changed but users complain. What happened?

Look at recall@1. In this chapter's condition B, fusion took recall@10 from
99.9% to 99.6% — nothing — while recall@1 went from **96.2% to 49.4%**. The
document was still retrieved; it was pushed down the list.

Which metric matters depends on the consumer. A RAG pipeline passing ten
chunks to a model cares about recall@10. A user reading the first result cares
about recall@1. Reporting only the one that looks good is the easiest
self-deception in retrieval.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Which embedding model should you use?

Not the famous one, and the difference only shows on hard inputs. A
*similarity* model and a *retrieval* model were within 2.4 points on the easy
condition here — and **25.3 points apart** on the hard one, 10.6% against
35.9%.

Similarity models are trained to score how alike two sentences are; retrieval
models are trained on query-document pairs with hard negatives. They are
different tasks. And the practical consequence for evaluation: if your test
set is easy, every model looks the same and you will pick by download count.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. Why is recall@k the number that bounds a RAG system?

Because a generator cannot ground an answer in a document it never received.
If recall@10 is 80% and you pass ten chunks, then 20% of questions are
ungroundable before the model is invoked, and prompt engineering cannot reach
them.

State the ceiling precisely, because it holds under conditions worth naming.
The model may still answer some of that 20% from its parametric knowledge, which
is not grounded in anything you retrieved. But a fact may also appear in a
document your relevance judgements did not happen to mark — and an answer
supported by *that* document is grounded in retrieved evidence, judgements or
no judgements. So recall@k bounds grounded answers when a single marked document
is the only place the fact appears and the judgements are complete. With
redundant evidence, incomplete judgements, or questions needing two passages at
once, document recall is not that bound in either direction. Measure end-to-end
answer accuracy separately for the number you actually want.

This is why the two stages want different metrics. Stage one is judged on not
missing; stage two — the reranker, or the generator — is judged on choosing
well from what arrived. Tuning stage one for precision@1 throws away the
recall the second stage needed.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Do you need a vector database?

Under about 100k documents, no — exhaustive search over a NumPy array is a
matrix multiply and it is exact. Up to roughly ten million, `pgvector` in the
Postgres you already run gives you transactions, backups, joins and access
control for free.

The thing that genuinely forces a dedicated store is rarely scale; it is
**filtered search** — the top ten documents this user may see, from the last
90 days, in this language — which needs the filter and the vector search to
cooperate. Weigh that against operating a second datastore with its own
consistency and backup story.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-retrieval-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** These recur in the two
credible open sources this book uses, plus the ones this chapter's own
measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the mechanism

**Q: Write down BM25 and explain what `k1` and `b` are doing.**

The scoring function is IDF times a saturating term frequency, with a length
correction:

$$
\text{BM25}(q,d) = \sum_{t \in q} \text{IDF}(t) \cdot
\frac{f_{t,d}\,(k_1+1)}{f_{t,d} + k_1\left(1 - b + b\,\frac{|d|}{\text{avgdl}}\right)}
$$

Here $f_{t,d}$ is how often term $t$ occurs in document $d$, $|d|$ is the
document's length and avgdl the average length in the collection. The IDF is
usually $\log\frac{N - n_t + 0.5}{n_t + 0.5}$ for $N$ documents of which $n_t$
contain $t$ (Lucene adds 1 inside the log so it never goes negative). Common
defaults are $k_1 \approx 1.2$–$2.0$ and $b = 0.75$.

The part worth saying out loud is *why* it saturates. In @sec-text-as-data's
TF-IDF with raw counts the tenth occurrence of a term counts exactly as much as
the first; here the term-frequency factor can never exceed $k_1+1$, and $k_1$
sets how fast it approaches that ceiling. With $k_1 = 1.2$ (and ignoring
length), a word used three times contributes 1.57 × IDF and a word used twenty
times only 2.08 × IDF — a third more, not seven times more — so repetition
cannot swamp a document that matches more of the query's other terms. And $b$
interpolates length normalisation: $b=0$ ignores document length, $b=1$
divides it out fully. If you add that `sublinear_tf` in `scikit-learn` is the
crude version of the same idea, you have connected the two chapters.

**Q: Bi-encoder or cross-encoder? Why not use the better one everywhere?**

A bi-encoder embeds query and document *independently*, so documents can be
encoded once, offline, and search is a vector operation. A cross-encoder reads
the pair jointly and scores it, which is strictly more informative and cannot
be precomputed — the cost is one forward pass per candidate at query time.
That is why the architecture is always both: retrieve a shortlist cheaply,
rerank it expensively. The follow-up to volunteer is where the shortlist
saturates, because reranking 1,000 candidates rarely buys more than reranking
100 and costs ten times as much.

**Q: What is the quality dial in an approximate index, and what is it set to
right now?**

`efSearch` in HNSW, `nprobe` in IVF — how much of the graph or how many
clusters get visited. The point of the question is the second half: it has a
default, the default was chosen by the library author and not by you, and it
is a *recall* setting wearing a performance costume. An ANN index that silently
returns 92% of the true neighbours has thrown away 8% of what exact search
would have found, before the model sees anything. Measure approximate against exhaustive on a sample and
you will know the number instead of assuming it.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: You are handed a corpus and no queries. How do you build an evaluation
set?**

Collect a hundred *real* queries — from logs, from support tickets, from the
people who will use it — because invented queries are systematically cleaner
than real ones and will flatter every system you test. Then pool: run two or
three different retrievers, label the union of their top-10, and you have
relevance judgements without reading the whole corpus. Say explicitly that a
hundred labelled queries beats a thousand unlabelled ones, and that the set is
worth more than any model choice you will make afterwards.

**Q: A stakeholder wants semantic search to replace keyword search. What do
you tell them?**

That the answer is an empirical question about their queries, and then show
them the two conditions from this chapter: on inflected keyword queries
stemmed BM25 scored **96.0%** recall@1 against a dense retriever's **35.9%**;
on cross-lingual queries the same dense model scored **96.2%** against BM25's
**23.8%**. Same corpus, opposite verdicts. So the real deliverable is a census
of their query mix, and if it is genuinely mixed, routing by query type beats
fusing — this chapter measured RRF *costing* 32.8 and 46.8 recall@1 points
against the better single retriever.

**Q: Retrieval looks good but the answers are bad. Whose problem is it?**

Do not guess — attribute. Check whether the supporting document was in the
top-k at all: if it was not, this is a retrieval problem and no prompting fixes
it; if it was, the model had what it needed and did not use it, which is a
grounding problem. @sec-rag builds that decomposition properly. The
one-sentence version, and the reason this chapter exists before that one:
recall@k is a *ceiling* on the whole system, so it is the first thing to
measure and the last thing you can fix by tuning a prompt.

## The 2026 toolbox {#sec-retrieval-tools}

Everything in this chapter ran on one laptop with the versions below.

| library | version used | what it is for here |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `sentence-transformers` | 6.0.0 | both dense models, and the encoding in @sec-retrieval-results |
| `snowballstemmer` | 3.1.1 | the Turkish stemmer that is worth 68 points in condition A |
| `numpy` | 2.5.2 | BM25, exhaustive dense search, and RRF — the whole retrieval stack in this chapter is a few hundred lines |

: The stack these numbers came from {tbl-colwidths="[26,14,60]"}

Worth knowing about, not used above:

| library | current version | when you would reach for it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `faiss-cpu` | 1.15.0 | HNSW and IVF-PQ indexes [@johnson2019billion]; the reference implementation, and where to sweep the recall/latency dial of @sec-retrieval-ann |
| `pgvector` | 0.5.0 | vectors in the database you already run — the default answer for most projects |
| `qdrant-client` / `chromadb` | 1.19.0 / 1.5.9 | dedicated stores, when filtered search at scale becomes the requirement |
| `rank-bm25` | 0.2.2 | BM25 without writing it yourself, for a quick baseline |
| `ir-measures` | 0.4.3 | the standard IR metrics computed the standard way, so your nDCG matches everyone else's definition of nDCG |

: The wider ecosystem, versions as of writing {tbl-colwidths="[24,16,60]"}

## Lab: build and tune a hybrid retriever {#sec-retrieval-lab}

Build both families on your own queries, then check the fusion before you
ship it rather than after.

### Step 1 — collect a hundred real queries

From logs if you have them, from users if you do not. This is the step that
decides everything else, because @sec-retrieval-results is one long
demonstration that the query distribution determines which retriever wins.

Classify them: exact-match (part numbers, names, codes), natural-language
questions, and anything crossing a language boundary.

### Step 2 — label relevance, then build BM25

For each query, the document that answers it. Fifty labelled queries is a
workable starting point for error analysis, but do not read it as enough to
*confirm* a ten-point gap. Do the arithmetic: ten points on fifty queries is
five extra successes, and even in the most favourable split — five gained, none
lost — a two-sided exact McNemar gives $p = 2/2^5 = 0.0625$, which does not
clear 5%. What it actually takes depends on the baseline
rate, on how correlated the two systems' errors are (a paired test on shared
queries needs far fewer than an unpaired one), and on how many comparisons you
plan to make. If the gap you care about is five points rather than ten, or the
systems agree on almost everything, budget for several hundred. Then build BM25 — and
if your language is morphologically rich, build it twice, with and without
stemming, because @sec-turkish-nlp says that one step can be worth more than
sixty points.

### Step 3 — add dense retrieval, with a retrieval model

Not a similarity model. Encode, search exhaustively — under 100k documents you
do not need an index yet — and report recall@1 and recall@10 next to BM25.

### Step 4 — check whether fusing helps *before* shipping it

Run RRF and compare against **the better parent**, not against the weaker one.
If the parents differ by more than about twenty points, expect fusion to hurt
and verify. The twenty is a rule of thumb, not a measured threshold: the gaps
measured in this chapter were sixty points and more. This is a fifteen-minute check that this chapter's measurements
suggest is skipped routinely.

### Step 5 — route instead, if your query mix is mixed

Classify the query and send it to the retriever that handles it. Measure the
router's accuracy separately from the retrievers', because a router error and
a retrieval error look identical in the final number and have different fixes.

### Step 6 — add a reranker and find where the shortlist saturates

Cross-encoder over the top 10, 25, 50, 100. Plot final accuracy against
latency. The shortlist size is a cleaner dial than any ANN parameter — but do
not assume the curve only goes up. A larger pool raises the *recall* the
reranker gets to work with, which is monotone; final accuracy is not, because
each extra candidate is also another chance for the reranker to score a
distractor above the right answer. Plot it rather than extrapolating it, and
expect a plateau or a slight decline past some size.

### What to hand in

One table of recall@1, recall@10 and nDCG@10 for every system on your own
queries, broken down **by query type**; the fusion check from step 4 with its
verdict; and a sentence naming the ceiling your first stage imposes on
everything downstream.

## Exercises {#sec-retrieval-exercises}

1. **Find the swap.** Build BM25 and a dense retriever on one corpus. Find
   three queries where each beats the other by a wide margin, and state the
   pattern in one sentence.

2. **Reproduce the fusion result.** Take two retrievers that differ by at
   least twenty points on your data and fuse them with RRF. Report recall@1
   and recall@10 for both parents and the fusion. Explain the shape of the
   damage.

3. **Weight the fusion.** Repeat exercise 2 with a weighted combination
   instead of plain RRF, tuning the weight on held-out queries. How much of
   the loss do you recover, and what did the tuning cost you in
   generalisation?

4. **Similarity model against retrieval model.** Run both on an easy query set
   and a hard one. Report the gap in each. Then say which set you would have
   used if you had only built one.

5. **The ANN dial.** Sweep `efSearch` or `nprobe`, and plot recall against p95
   latency — measuring recall against *exhaustive search*, not against your
   labels, so you separate index loss from embedding error.

6. **Recall as a ceiling.** Measure recall@k on your retriever for k = 1, 5,
   10, 25. For each, state the maximum accuracy a downstream generator could
   achieve. Compare against what your RAG system actually achieves, and say
   where the remaining gap lives.

7. **Query-type census.** Sample 100 production queries and classify them.
   Predict, from this chapter's tables, which retriever should win your mix.
   Then measure and see whether you were right.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-retrieval-deeper}

Do this first: take twenty real queries and check whether the right document
is in the top ten. That number is the ceiling on everything you build
afterwards, and most teams have never measured it.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [Introduction to Information Retrieval](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/) — Manning, Raghavan, Schütze | free, and still the best foundation; the chapters on indexing and evaluation have not aged |
| [Sentence Transformers](https://sbert.net/) | the practical guide to bi-encoders, cross-encoders and when each is appropriate |
| [Pinecone Learn](https://www.pinecone.io/learn/) | vendor-published but genuinely good explainers on ANN indexes and hybrid search |
| [`faiss`](https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss) | the reference ANN library; its wiki explains the recall/latency dial better than most papers |
| [ColBERT](https://github.com/stanford-futuredata/ColBERT) | late interaction, the middle path between the two architectures in @sec-retrieval-reranking |

## What to remember {#sec-retrieval-summary}

- **Neither retrieval family dominates, and the query type decides.** Same
  corpus, two query conditions: stemmed BM25 **96.0%** against dense **35.9%**
  on keyword queries; dense **96.2%** against BM25 **23.8%** cross-lingually.
  A retrieval number without its query distribution is not interpretable.

- **Unweighted RRF is not free, and it is not always positive.** It cost
  **32.8** and **46.8** recall@1 points against the better parent in the two
  conditions, because rank fusion weights a rank-1 hit from a weak system like a
  rank-1 hit from a strong one. Note the word *unweighted*: rank fusion discards
  score magnitude, which is the only signal that separates a
  confident-and-right system from a confident-and-wrong one. Weighted RRF does
  not recover it: it still fuses ranks, and only scales each system's
  contribution by a fixed weight. Score-normalised fusion [@bruch2024fusion]
  uses the scores themselves. Each needs one fitted parameter, and neither was
  measured here.

- **The damage lands on recall@1, not recall@10.** In condition B, fusion took
  R@10 from 99.9% to 99.6% and R@1 from 96.2% to 49.4%. Which metric you watch
  determines whether you notice.

- **Fuse comparable systems; route mixed query loads.** If one retriever
  dominates on your queries, use it. If your users send both kinds, classify
  the query and dispatch — and evaluate the router separately.

- **A similarity model is not a retrieval model.** The two were 2.4 points
  apart on the easy condition and **25.3** apart on the hard one. Component
  quality only becomes visible on the inputs that are hard for that component,
  which is an argument for keeping a difficult slice in your evaluation.

- **Hard negatives are the whole game in dense training.** In-batch negatives
  teach topical separation; mined hard negatives teach the distinction your
  users need. Re-mine as the model improves, and mine slightly below the top
  of the list to avoid training against unlabelled relevant documents.

- **Retrieve broadly, rerank precisely.** A cross-encoder is usually more accurate and
  cannot be precomputed, so it reorders a shortlist. It can only reorder what
  stage one returned — **the first stage sets a ceiling the second cannot
  raise**.

- **Report recall@k for the k you actually pass downstream.** It bounds what
  any RAG system can ground: a generator cannot ground an answer in a document
  it never received. With one relevant document per question, 80% recall@10
  means 20% of questions cannot be grounded in retrieved evidence before
  generation starts (the model may still answer some from memory, ungrounded).

- **Keep the vectors where the data is until scale forces otherwise.** Under
  100k documents, exhaustive search is exact and instant. What eventually
  forces a dedicated store is filtered search at scale, not raw volume.
